raw_case_text: A 34-year-old woman was admitted to our center with complaints of lower abdominal pain, anorexia, constipation, and significant weight loss (more than 10 Kg during 4 months). There was no history of fever, nausea, or vomiting. Habitual and occupational history was uneventful. She had 3 normal full-term deliveries. As the patient had severe constipation and other gastrointestinal symptoms, colonoscopy had been carried out in another center with normal findings.  On pelvic examination a nontender, uniformly cystic mass approximately 28-week size was palpated. Speculum examination was normal. Laboratory investigations including blood sugar, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, liver enzymes, and urinalysis were normal and stool occult blood was negative. Pregnancy test was negative. Complete blood count was normal except mild anemia (Hb: 7 gr/dL). Chest radiograph was also normal. On transabdominal ultrasound, multiple anechoic masses were demonstrated in the pelvic and uterine cavities. For further delineation of the cystic masses and disease extension in the pelvic cavity, computed tomography (CT) scan was performed, that revealing multiple cystic space-occupying lesions in the pelvic cavity, involving the uterus, broad ligament, and adnexa (Figure 1). The patient underwent an exploratory laparotomy under general anesthesia for further diagnosis of the cystic mass, and ruling out of the genitourinary malignancy. Preoperative laboratory evaluation including HIV antibody, VDRL test, HBS antigen, and HCV antibody assay were normal. Additionally, whole body bone scan, chest and abdominal CT scan were also performed that revealed unremarkable results. On the 10th day of her admission after obtaining the informed consent, the patient underwent surgical exploration. At the operation, numerous ovarian and paraovarian cystic masses densely adhered to the uterus, to the pelvic side wall, and to the fallopian tubes were demonstrated. One of the cysts was removed completely and sent to the laboratory and this surgical specimen was diagnosed as the hydatid cyst. Due to extensive involvement of the uterus, adnexa, and broad ligament, complete removal of the cysts and preservation of the all reproductive organs was impossible; furthermore complete removal of the cysts due to the high risk of rupture could be life threatening, so after obtaining the signed consent we decided to perform removal of the cysts of the right adnexa and uterus with preservation of them and left side salpingoophorectomy. The rest of the abdomen and pelvis were free of pathology. The abdomen was then carefully irrigated with isotonic saline. Microscopic examination disclosed the scolices of Echinococcus granulosis with adjacent laminated membrane and confirmed the diagnosis (Figure 2). The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged on the 11th postoperative day. Albendazole (800 mg per day) as adjuvant therapy was administered for 4 months postoperatively. Blood count and liver transaminases were checked during the course of therapy which showed normal results. At 6-month follow-up the patient was doing well with no detectable abnormality on follow-up ultrasound.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old woman presented with a 4-month history of lower abdominal pain, anorexia, severe constipation, and weight loss exceeding 10 kg.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed progressive lower abdominal pain, anorexia, severe constipation, and >10 kg weight loss over 4 months. An outside colonoscopy performed for her gastrointestinal symptoms was normal.
subjective.past_medical_history: Gravida 3, para 3 with three normal full-term deliveries; unremarkable occupational and habitual history; normal prior colonoscopy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for lower abdominal pain, anorexia, severe constipation, and >10 kg weight loss; negative for fever, nausea, or vomiting.

objective.physical_examination: Pelvic examination revealed a non-tender, uniformly cystic abdominopelvic mass corresponding to a 28-week gravid uterus size; speculum examination was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count was normal except for anemia (hemoglobin 7 g/dL). Blood glucose, BUN, creatinine, liver enzymes, urinalysis, stool occult blood, pregnancy test, HIV antibody, VDRL, HBsAg, and HCV antibody were normal/negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Transabdominal ultrasound showed multiple anechoic cystic masses in the pelvic and uterine cavities.
objective.advanced_workup: Pelvic CT demonstrated multiple cystic space-occupying lesions involving the uterus, broad ligament, and adnexa, while chest CT, abdominal CT, and whole-body bone scan were normal. Exploratory laparotomy on hospital day 10 revealed numerous ovarian and paraovarian cysts densely adherent to the uterus, pelvic sidewalls, and fallopian tubes; cyst excision from the uterus and right adnexa with organ preservation and left salpingo-oophorectomy were performed, and microscopic examination identified Echinococcus granulosus scolices and an adjacent laminated membrane.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary pelvic and genital hydatidosis involving the uterus, broad ligament, and bilateral adnexa, confirmed by histopathological visualization of Echinococcus granulosus scolices and laminated membrane (ruling out genitourinary malignancy). Following surgical resection of the uterine and right adnexal cysts with left salpingo-oophorectomy and isotonic saline peritoneal irrigation, the patient was discharged on postoperative day 11 and completed 4 months of adjuvant oral albendazole (800 mg/day) with normal CBC and transaminase monitoring, remaining asymptomatic with a normal ultrasound at 6-month follow-up.
